title: Undak usuk basa — the heart of Sundanese
goal: Master the speech-level system as a whole: three columns, one golden rule, and a quick way to choose in the middle of a conversation. Every later unit rests on this one.
bekal: tell apart basa loma, lemes keur sorangan (polite, for yourself), and lemes ka batur (polite, for others)
the golden rule: column three is never for yourself
all the personal pronouns at both levels, and why terms of address are safer

dialogs.title: Paguneman — A lesson from Bu Imas
dialogs.intro: Sunday morning. Rani is sitting in the boarding house's living room with a notebook. Bu Imas is folding laundry and decides it is time for the first lesson.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Néng, ayeuna Ibu badé ngajar nu paling penting.
lines.id: Néng, today I'm going to teach you the most important thing.
lines.literal: Néng, now Ma'am will teach which most important.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Please do, ma'am. What is it?

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Undak usuk. Cobi, kumaha nyebat "saya mau makan"?
lines.id: Undak usuk. Let's see — how do you say "I want to eat"?
lines.literal: undak usuk. try, how say "I want to-eat"?

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Nah, éta anu lepat. Tuang mah kanggo batur, sanés kanggo diri sorangan.
lines.id: There — that's the mistake. Tuang is for other people, not for yourself.
lines.literal: there, that which wrong. tuang [mah] for others, not for self own.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Abdi badé neda. Neda kanggo diri, tuang kanggo batur nu dihormat.
lines.id: Abdi badé neda. Neda is for yourself, tuang is for people you respect.
lines.literal: I will neda. neda for self, tuang for others who respected.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Janten aya tilu, nya? Dahar, neda, tuang.
lines.id: So there are three, right? Dahar, neda, tuang.
lines.literal: so there-are three, [nya]? dahar, neda, tuang.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Leres pisan. Dahar kanggo babaturan, neda kanggo diri, tuang kanggo nu luhur.
lines.id: Exactly. Dahar for friends, neda for yourself, tuang for those above you.
lines.literal: right very. dahar for friends, neda for self, tuang for who high.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: Are all words like that, ma'am?

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Henteu sadaya. Ngan kecap sapopoé: dahar, saré, indit, balik, mandi.
lines.id: Not all. Just everyday words: eat, sleep, go, go home, bathe.
lines.literal: not all. only words everyday: eat, sleep, go, return, bathe.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.id: I think I'll make lots of mistakes at first.

lines.speaker: Bu Imas:
lines.text: Teu nanaon. Nu penting daék diajar. Urang Sunda mah ngartos ka nu keur diajar.
lines.id: That's fine. What matters is being willing to learn. Sundanese people understand learners.
lines.literal: not anything. which important willing learn. people Sundanese [mah] understand to who are learning.

lines.speaker: Rani:
lines.text: Hatur nuhun, Bu. Abdi bade nyatet heula.
lines.id: Thank you, ma'am. Let me write it down first.
lines.literal: thank-you, Ma'am. I will note-down first.

notes: **Undak usuk basa** literally means "the steps of language". The name fits: it really is a staircase, and each speaker stands on a different step depending on age, status, and closeness. Javanese (*ngoko–krama*) and Balinese have similar systems; English has **nothing** like it — the nearest thing is choosing between "hey, grab a seat" and "please, do sit down", except that in Sundanese the choice is built into the words themselves. That is why it needs a whole unit.
**Kanggo** = for (lemes). The loma form is **keur** — which also means "in the middle of (doing)". Context tells them apart: *keur dahar* = eating right now, *keur saha?* = for whom?
**Lepat** = wrong (lemes); the loma form is **salah**. The opposite is *leres* (lemes) / *bener* (loma).
**Janten** = so, therefore; to become (lemes). The loma form is **jadi**. It is also a short answer meaning "it's on" or "OK": *Janten teu?* = is it still on?
**Daék** = willing (loma); the lemes form is **kersa**. It differs from *hayang/hoyong*, which mean wanting something. *Daék diajar* = willing to learn; *hayang dahar* = want to eat.
**Sigana** = it seems, probably. From *siga* (like, resembling). Very common and very useful for softening a statement: *sigana hujan* = looks like rain.
**Sadaya** = all (lemes); loma: **kabéh** or **sadayana**. *Sadayana*, with *-na*, is used when it stands alone: *Sadayana sami* = they're all the same.

grammars.title: Three columns and one golden rule
body: Imagine every everyday verb has three cards. You choose the card not by meaning — the meaning is the same — but by **who is doing it** and **who is listening**.
Here are the three columns, with their official names and what they are used for:

head: Column
Official name
Used for
Spoken to
rows: friends your age, younger people, people you're close to

after: **GOLDEN RULE: column 3 is never for yourself.** It is the one rule that, if broken, really sounds wrong. Using column 3 about yourself means you are raising yourself up — which in Sundanese manners is worse than being blunt.
The reverse also matters: using column 2 about someone else lowers them. *Ibu badé neda?* sounds as if you are putting Ma'am on the level of a servant. The right form: *Ibu badé tuang?*

If you get stuck mid-conversation, the way out is always **column 1 with a polite tone and the right term of address**. Speaking loma while calling the other person *Ibu* is far better than using column 3 about yourself. Sundanese people forgive a lack of polish; they are uncomfortable with people who raise themselves up.

grammars.title: The core list — twenty must-know words
body: Only everyday words have three forms. Hundreds of others — *maca* (read), *nulis* (write), *lumpat* (run) — are the same at every level. The twenty rows below cover most A1 conversation:
after: Notice that some rows have the **same** word in columns 2 and 3 (*ngaleueut*, *nyandak*, *damel*, *ngadangu*). That makes life easier — those words are safe in both directions.

Some nouns have levels too; these are the ones you will meet most: **imah / rorompok / bumi** (house), **ngaran / nami / jenengan** (name), **umur / yuswa / yuswa** (age), **anak / putra / putra** (child), **duit / artos / artos** (money), **awak / salira / salira** (body).

⚠️ Pay attention to **bumi**: in Sundanese it means **house** (of someone you respect), not the planet, as it does in Indonesian. *Bumi Ibu di mana?* = "where is your house, ma'am?" When you answer about your own home, use **rorompok**: *Rorompok abdi di Dago.*

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Aing** and **sia** are rude pronouns. Both are very much alive — you will hear them between close friends, on the football field, and from the mouth of Cepot, the clown of the *wayang golék* puppet show. As a newcomer, **don't use them at all**, at least until you have friends who use them with you first.

Far more important than memorizing this table: in real Bandung conversation, the word "you" is **often avoided altogether**. Not because it is complicated, but because calling people by a term of address feels warmer.

head: Not this
But this
Meaning
rows: Have you eaten? (to an older woman)

blocks.title: Possession: -na, and no word for "your"
items: Sundanese has no suffix for "your". You show it by naming the person's term of address: **bumi Ibu** (your house, ma'am), **buku Aa** (your book, said to Aa).
The suffix **-na** = his/her/its/the: *imahna* (his/her house), *ngaranna* (his/her name), *hargana* (the price).
"My": put **abdi** / **kuring** after the noun — *buku abdi* (my book), *imah kuring* (my house). There is no separate "my" suffix.
⚠️ **-na** is also used to point to a specific thing, much like "the": *hargana sabaraha?* = "how much is it?" (literally "the price how much?") even when no owner is mentioned.

blocks.text: In the middle of a conversation you have no time to open a table. Ask yourself these three questions in order; the answers settle the level in seconds.

items: **One — is the person I'm talking to older or someone to respect?** If yes, the whole sentence is lemes. If not, loma is fine.
**Two — who is doing the action?** If it's me, use column 2. If it's them, use column 3.
**Three — not sure?** Use column 1 with the right term of address. Safe, and never offensive.

blocks.text: A worked example: the same sentence in five situations:

head: Situation
Sentence
Column
rows: To Bu Imas, about Bu Imas
To a friend, about Bu Imas
To a friend, about another friend

blocks.text: Row four matters: the level depends on **the person being talked about**, not only on the listener. Even when chatting casually with a friend, you still use column 3 for someone you respect.

blocks.title: The five most common newcomer mistakes
items: ❌ *Abdi bumina di Dago.* → ✅ **Rorompok abdi di Dago.**

Kuring rék ____ ka Dago. (go, to a friend)

Abdi tos ____ tabuh sapuluh. (sleep, about yourself, lemes)
